questions.stem:
(a) Define accounting. [3 marks]
(b) Identify four users of accounting information and state the information each needs. [8 marks]
(c) Explain two qualitative characteristics of useful accounting information. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) The process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising and communicating financial information about an entity to enable users to make informed decisions (3)
8 marks: (b) Any four users with need, 2 marks each: owners/shareholders (profitability, returns, stewardship); lenders/banks (ability to repay loans and interest); suppliers/creditors (ability to pay debts on time); employees/trade unions (stability, ability to pay wages); government/tax authorities (taxable profit, statistics); customers (continuity of supply); investors/analysts (future prospects); management (planning and control)
4 marks: (c) Any two, 2 marks each: relevance (capable of influencing decisions, timely); reliability/faithful representation (free from error and bias, complete, neutral); comparability (can be compared over time and with other entities); understandability (clear to users with reasonable knowledge)
questions.explanation: (a) Accounting is the process of identifying, recording, classifying, summarising and communicating financial information to help users make decisions. (b) Owners need information on profit and stewardship; lenders need evidence of ability to repay; suppliers want to know whether they will be paid; employees look for stability and ability to pay wages; government needs profit figures for tax and statistics. (c) Useful information is relevant, meaning it can influence decisions and is timely, and reliable, meaning it is free from material error and bias; it should also be comparable and understandable.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain, with an example each, the following accounting concepts: (i) going concern; (ii) prudence; (iii) accruals; (iv) business entity; (v) consistency. [10 marks]
(b) State two limitations of accounting concepts. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) Going concern: business assumed to continue operating for the foreseeable future, so assets are valued at cost less depreciation rather than forced-sale value (1 + 1 example)
2 marks: (a)(ii) Prudence: losses provided for as soon as anticipated, gains recognised only when realised, e.g. provision for doubtful debts, stock at lower of cost and net realisable value (1 + 1)
2 marks: (a)(iii) Accruals: revenue and expenses recognised when earned or incurred, not when cash is received or paid, e.g. accrued rent included as expense (1 + 1)
2 marks: (a)(iv) Business entity: business treated as separate from its owner, e.g. owner's private expenses recorded as drawings (1 + 1)
2 marks: (a)(v) Consistency: same accounting methods applied from period to period, e.g. same depreciation method each year (1 + 1)
5 marks: (b) Any two (2.5 marks each): historical cost ignores inflation/changing prices; money measurement ignores non-monetary factors such as staff skill; concepts may conflict (e.g. prudence vs accruals); allow subjective judgement; may be manipulated (creative accounting)
questions.explanation: (a) Going concern assumes the business will continue, so assets are shown at cost less depreciation. Prudence means anticipating losses but not gains, as in providing for doubtful debts. Accruals matches income and expenses with the period in which they arise, so unpaid rent is still charged. Business entity separates the owner from the business, so his private spending is drawings. Consistency requires methods such as depreciation to be applied the same way each year. (b) Concepts based on historical cost ignore inflation, money measurement leaves out non-financial factors, concepts can conflict and they leave room for judgement.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem:
On 31 March, the bank column of the cash book of Ojo Enterprises showed a debit balance of ₦246,500, while the bank statement on the same date showed a credit balance of ₦221,300. A comparison revealed the following:
1. Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment: ₦38,000 and ₦21,500.
2. A lodgement of ₦45,000 made on 31 March had not been credited by the bank.
3. Bank charges of ₦2,700 had not been entered in the cash book.
4. A standing order for insurance of ₦15,000 had not been entered in the cash book.
5. A dividend of ₦12,000 was received directly by the bank but not entered in the cash book.
6. A customer's cheque for ₦34,000 had been dishonoured, but this was not recorded in the cash book.
(a) Prepare the adjusted cash book (bank column) balance. [7 marks]
(b) Prepare a bank reconciliation statement as at 31 March. [6 marks]
(c) State one reason for preparing a bank reconciliation statement. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
7 marks: (a) Balance b/d 246,500 (1); add dividend 12,000 (1); less bank charges 2,700 (1), insurance standing order 15,000 (1), dishonoured cheque 34,000 (1); adjusted balance ₦206,800 (2)
6 marks: (b) Balance per adjusted cash book 206,800 (1); add unpresented cheques 59,500 (2); less uncredited lodgement 45,000 (2); balance per bank statement ₦221,300 (1)
2 marks: (c) Any one: to explain differences between cash book and bank statement; to detect errors/omissions; to update the cash book; to detect fraud (2)
questions.explanation: (a) Adjusted cash book = 246,500 + 12,000 − 2,700 − 15,000 − 34,000 = ₦206,800 debit. (b) Starting from the adjusted cash book balance of ₦206,800, add cheques not yet presented (38,000 + 21,500 = 59,500) because the bank has not yet deducted them, and deduct the uncredited lodgement of ₦45,000 because the bank has not yet added it: 206,800 + 59,500 − 45,000 = ₦221,300, agreeing with the bank statement. (c) The statement explains the difference between the two records and helps detect errors, omissions and fraud.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem:
The trial balance of Eze Traders failed to agree, and the difference was entered in a suspense account. The following errors were later found:
(i) The sales day book was overcast by ₦3,000.
(ii) Discount received of ₦1,800 was correctly entered in the creditors' accounts but not posted to the discount received account.
(iii) Rent paid of ₦12,500 was posted to the rent account as ₦21,500.
(iv) Equipment bought for ₦60,000 was debited to the purchases account.
(v) Cash of ₦14,000 received from Bello was credited to the account of Bella.
(a) Prepare journal entries to correct the errors (narrations not required). [6 marks]
(b) Calculate the original difference in the trial balance and state on which side of the suspense account it was entered. [3 marks]
(c) Prepare the suspense account. [3 marks]
(d) The net profit before the corrections was ₦250,000. Calculate the corrected net profit (ignore depreciation). [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) (i) Dr Sales 3,000, Cr Suspense 3,000; (ii) Dr Suspense 1,800, Cr Discount received 1,800; (iii) Dr Suspense 9,000, Cr Rent 9,000; (iv) Dr Equipment 60,000, Cr Purchases 60,000; (v) Dr Bella 14,000, Cr Bello 14,000 (1 mark each, plus 1 for correct amounts throughout)
3 marks: (b) Debit side exceeded credit side by 9,000 + 1,800 − 3,000 = ₦7,800 (2); entered on the credit side of suspense (1)
3 marks: (c) Suspense: Cr balance b/d 7,800 and Cr sales correction 3,000; Dr discount received 1,800 and Dr rent 9,000; both sides total ₦10,800 (3)
3 marks: (d) 250,000 − 3,000 + 1,800 + 9,000 + 60,000 (2) = ₦317,800 (1)
questions.explanation: (a) The corrections are: debit sales and credit suspense ₦3,000; debit suspense and credit discount received ₦1,800; debit suspense and credit rent ₦9,000; debit equipment and credit purchases ₦60,000; debit Bella and credit Bello ₦14,000. (b) Errors (ii) and (iii) made the debit side ₦10,800 too large relative to credits and error (i) made credits ₦3,000 too large, so debits exceeded credits by ₦7,800, and suspense was opened with a credit balance of ₦7,800. (c) The suspense account has credits of 7,800 and 3,000 and debits of 1,800 and 9,000, totalling ₦10,800 each and closing to nil. Errors (iv) and (v) did not affect the trial balance. (d) Corrected profit = 250,000 − 3,000 + 1,800 + 9,000 + 60,000 = ₦317,800.

questions.topic: The Final Accounts of a Sole Trader/Proprietorship
questions.stem:
The following balances were extracted from the books of Amaka Stores on 31 December:
Sales 2,450,000; Purchases 1,520,000; Stock 1 January 210,000; Returns inwards 40,000; Returns outwards 25,000; Carriage inwards 18,000; Wages and salaries 285,000; Rent 120,000; Electricity 46,000; Insurance 36,000; Carriage outwards 22,000; Discount allowed 9,000; Discount received 6,000; Bad debts 7,000; Motor van (cost) 900,000; Furniture (cost) 300,000; Debtors 260,000; Creditors 185,000; Cash at bank 154,000; Drawings 120,000; Capital 1,381,000.
Adjustments: (1) Stock at 31 December ₦245,000. (2) Wages accrued ₦15,000. (3) Insurance prepaid ₦9,000. (4) Depreciate the motor van at 20% and furniture at 10% on cost. (5) Create a provision for doubtful debts of 5% of debtors.
(a) Calculate cost of goods sold and gross profit. [5 marks]
(b) Calculate the total expenses and net profit for the year. [5 marks]
(c) Calculate the totals of non-current assets, current assets and current liabilities, and show that net assets equal closing capital. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: (a) Net sales are ₦2,410,000. Cost of goods sold = 210,000 + 1,520,000 − 25,000 + 18,000 − 245,000 = ₦1,478,000, so gross profit is ₦932,000. (b) Expenses after adjustments are wages ₦300,000 (285,000 + 15,000), rent ₦120,000, electricity ₦46,000, insurance ₦27,000 (36,000 − 9,000), carriage outwards ₦22,000, discount allowed ₦9,000, bad debts ₦7,000, depreciation ₦180,000 and ₦30,000, and provision for doubtful debts ₦13,000: total ₦754,000. Net profit = 932,000 + 6,000 − 754,000 = ₦184,000. (c) Non-current assets: van 720,000 + furniture 270,000 = ₦990,000. Current assets: stock 245,000, net debtors 247,000, prepaid insurance 9,000, bank 154,000 = ₦655,000. Current liabilities: creditors 185,000 + accrued wages 15,000 = ₦200,000. Net assets = 990,000 + 655,000 − 200,000 = ₦1,445,000, equal to capital 1,381,000 + 184,000 − 120,000.

questions.stem:

Machine A was sold on 30 June Year 4 for ₦350,000. The financial year ends on 31 December.
(a) Calculate the depreciation charge for each of Years 1 to 4. [4 marks]
(b) Prepare the machine disposal account. [5 marks]
(c) Calculate the balance on the provision for depreciation account at 31 December Year 4. [3 marks]
(d) State three causes of depreciation. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Year 1 ₦160,000; Year 2 ₦260,000; Year 3 ₦260,000; Year 4 ₦100,000 (1 mark each)
5 marks: (b) Dr machine (cost) 800,000 (1); Cr provision for depreciation 480,000 (1); Cr bank/proceeds 350,000 (1); profit on disposal ₦30,000 debited to disposal and credited to income statement (2)
3 marks: (c) 160,000 + 260,000 + 260,000 + 100,000 − 480,000 (2) = ₦300,000, all relating to Machine B (1)
3 marks: (d) Any three, 1 mark each: wear and tear; obsolescence; passage of time; depletion; inadequacy; accidents
questions.explanation: (a) Machine A attracts ₦160,000 a year and Machine B ₦100,000 a year: Year 1 ₦160,000; Year 2 ₦260,000; Year 3 ₦260,000; Year 4 only Machine B, ₦100,000, as no charge is made on A in its year of sale. (b) Machine A had accumulated depreciation of 3 x 160,000 = ₦480,000, so its book value was ₦320,000; sold for ₦350,000, it gave a profit of ₦30,000, shown in the disposal account with the cost on the debit side and depreciation and proceeds on the credit side. (c) The provision stands at 160,000 + 260,000 + 260,000 + 100,000 − 480,000 = ₦300,000, being three years on Machine B. (d) Depreciation is caused by wear and tear, obsolescence, the passage of time and depletion.

(d) Cost of production = 1,073,000 + 235,000 + opening WIP 40,000 − closing WIP 52,000 = ₦1,296,000. (e) Unit cost = 1,296,000/20,000 = ₦64.80.

From the following information for the year, prepare (a) the sales ledger control account and (b) the purchases ledger control account of Lawal & Sons.
Sales ledger debit balances 1 January ₦184,000; credit balances 1 January ₦3,500
Credit sales ₦1,260,000
Cash and cheques received from customers ₦1,082,000
Discount allowed ₦21,000
Returns inwards ₦34,000
Bad debts written off ₦11,500
Customers' cheques dishonoured ₦8,000
Interest charged on overdue accounts ₦2,400
Contra (set-off) against purchases ledger ₦15,000
Sales ledger credit balances 31 December ₦4,200
Purchases ledger credit balances 1 January ₦126,000
Credit purchases ₦890,000
Payments to suppliers ₦812,000
Discount received ₦13,500
Returns outwards ₦22,000
(a) Sales ledger control account, showing the closing debit balance. [10 marks]
(b) Purchases ledger control account, showing the closing credit balance. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: (a) Debit side: balance b/d 184,000, credit sales 1,260,000, dishonoured cheques 8,000, interest charged 2,400, credit balances c/d 4,200 (total 1,458,600) (4); credit side: balance b/d 3,500, cash 1,082,000, discount allowed 21,000, returns inwards 34,000, bad debts 11,500, contra 15,000 (3); closing debit balance c/d ₦291,600 (3)
5 marks: (b) Debit: payments 812,000, discount received 13,500, returns outwards 22,000, contra 15,000 (2); credit: balance b/d 126,000, credit purchases 890,000 (1); closing credit balance c/d ₦153,500 (2)
questions.explanation: (a) The sales ledger control account is debited with the opening debit balances (184,000), credit sales (1,260,000), dishonoured cheques (8,000), interest charged (2,400) and the closing credit balances carried down (4,200), totalling ₦1,458,600; it is credited with opening credit balances (3,500), receipts (1,082,000), discount allowed (21,000), returns inwards (34,000), bad debts (11,500) and the contra (15,000), totalling ₦1,167,000. The closing debit balance is therefore ₦291,600. (b) The purchases ledger control account has credits of 126,000 + 890,000 = ₦1,016,000 and debits of 812,000 + 13,500 + 22,000 + 15,000 = ₦862,500, leaving a closing credit balance of ₦153,500.

questions.stem:
Kemi keeps incomplete records. Her position on 1 January was: shop fittings ₦180,000; stock ₦95,000; debtors ₦64,000; bank ₦38,000; creditors ₦52,000; rent accrued ₦6,000.
Her bank summary for the year showed: receipts from debtors ₦742,000; cash sales banked ₦186,000; payments to creditors ₦568,000; rent ₦54,000; wages ₦96,000; drawings ₦72,000; general expenses ₦31,000.
On 31 December: stock ₦108,000; debtors ₦79,000; creditors ₦61,000; rent prepaid ₦3,000. Discounts allowed were ₦6,000 and discounts received ₦4,000. Shop fittings are to be depreciated by 10%.
Calculate:
(a) Kemi's capital on 1 January [3 marks]
(b) credit sales and total sales for the year [3 marks]
(c) credit purchases for the year [2 marks]
(d) gross profit [3 marks]
(e) net profit [4 marks]
questions.explanation: (a) Opening capital = 180,000 + 95,000 + 64,000 + 38,000 − 52,000 − 6,000 = ₦319,000. (b) Credit sales = receipts 742,000 + discount 6,000 + closing debtors 79,000 − opening debtors 64,000 = ₦763,000; adding cash sales of ₦186,000 gives total sales of ₦949,000. (c) Credit purchases = 568,000 + 4,000 + 61,000 − 52,000 = ₦581,000. (d) Cost of goods sold = 95,000 + 581,000 − 108,000 = ₦568,000, giving gross profit of ₦381,000. (e) Rent for the year is 54,000 − 6,000 (last year's accrual) − 3,000 (prepaid) = ₦45,000; with wages 96,000, general expenses 31,000, depreciation 18,000 and discount allowed 6,000, expenses total ₦196,000; net profit = 381,000 + 4,000 − 196,000 = ₦189,000.

questions.stem:
The following information relates to the Unity Social Club for the year ended 31 December.
Balances at 1 January: clubhouse ₦2,500,000; equipment ₦340,000; bar stock ₦45,000; cash ₦62,000; subscriptions in arrears ₦24,000; subscriptions in advance ₦8,000; electricity accrued ₦11,000.
During the year subscriptions received were ₦410,000. At 31 December subscriptions in arrears were ₦30,000 and in advance ₦12,000.
Bar sales were ₦380,000, bar purchases ₦236,000 and bar stock at 31 December ₦52,000.
(a) Calculate the subscriptions to be credited to the income and expenditure account. [5 marks]
(b) Calculate the accumulated fund at 1 January. [5 marks]
(c) Calculate the profit on the bar. [3 marks]
(d) State one difference between a receipts and payments account and an income and expenditure account. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) Subscriptions account: Cr in advance b/d 8,000, cash 410,000, arrears c/d 30,000 (2); Dr arrears b/d 24,000, in advance c/d 12,000 (1); income and expenditure = ₦412,000 (2)
5 marks: (b) Assets 2,500,000 + 340,000 + 45,000 + 62,000 + 24,000 = 2,971,000 (2); liabilities 8,000 + 11,000 = 19,000 (1); accumulated fund ₦2,952,000 (2)
3 marks: (c) Cost of bar sales 45,000 + 236,000 − 52,000 = 229,000 (2); bar profit ₦151,000 (1)
2 marks: (d) Any one: R&P records actual cash receipts and payments while I&E follows the accruals basis; R&P includes capital items, I&E only revenue items; R&P shows cash balance, I&E shows surplus or deficit (2)
questions.explanation: (a) Subscription income = 410,000 + 8,000 (opening in advance) + 30,000 (closing arrears) − 24,000 (opening arrears) − 12,000 (closing in advance) = ₦412,000. (b) Assets total ₦2,971,000 and liabilities (subscriptions in advance and accrued electricity) ₦19,000, so the accumulated fund is ₦2,952,000. (c) Cost of bar sales = 45,000 + 236,000 − 52,000 = ₦229,000; bar profit = 380,000 − 229,000 = ₦151,000. (d) A receipts and payments account is a cash summary including capital items, while an income and expenditure account is prepared on the accruals basis for revenue items and shows a surplus or deficit.

questions.stem:
Ade and Bisi are partners sharing profits and losses in the ratio 3:2. Their fixed capitals are Ade ₦1,200,000 and Bisi ₦800,000. The partnership agreement provides for interest on capital at 10% per annum and a salary of ₦150,000 to Bisi. Interest on drawings for the year was Ade ₦9,000 and Bisi ₦6,000. Net profit for the year was ₦865,000. Drawings were Ade ₦180,000 and Bisi ₦120,000. Current account balances at the start of the year were Ade ₦40,000 credit and Bisi ₦15,000 debit.
(a) Prepare the profit and loss appropriation account. [8 marks]
(b) Calculate the closing balance on each partner's current account. [7 marks]
questions.explanation: (a) Profit available = 865,000 + 15,000 interest on drawings = ₦880,000. Interest on capital is ₦120,000 for Ade and ₦80,000 for Bisi, and Bisi's salary is ₦150,000, leaving ₦530,000 shared 3:2: Ade ₦318,000 and Bisi ₦212,000. (b) Ade's current account: 40,000 + 120,000 + 318,000 − 180,000 − 9,000 = ₦289,000 credit. Bisi's: opening debit 15,000, so −15,000 + 80,000 + 150,000 + 212,000 − 120,000 − 6,000 = ₦301,000 credit.

questions.stem:
Femi and Gbenga share profits 3:2 with capitals of ₦900,000 and ₦600,000 respectively. They admit Halima as a partner for a one-quarter share; Femi and Gbenga will share the remaining three-quarters in their old ratio. Halima brings in ₦700,000 as capital. Goodwill is valued at ₦400,000, but no goodwill account is to remain in the books. Before admission, premises are revalued upwards by ₦150,000, stock is reduced by ₦30,000 and a provision for doubtful debts of ₦10,000 is created.
(a) Calculate the profit on revaluation and each old partner's share. [4 marks]
(b) Calculate the new profit-sharing ratio. [3 marks]
(c) Show the adjustments for goodwill in the partners' capital accounts. [4 marks]
(d) Calculate the capital of each partner after Halima's admission. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) 150,000 − 30,000 − 10,000 = ₦110,000 (2); Femi ₦66,000, Gbenga ₦44,000 (2)
3 marks: (b) Femi 3/4 x 3/5 = 9/20; Gbenga 3/4 x 2/5 = 6/20; Halima 5/20; ratio 9:6:5 (3)
4 marks: (c) Goodwill raised in old ratio: Femi Cr 240,000, Gbenga Cr 160,000 (2); written off in new ratio: Femi Dr 180,000, Gbenga Dr 120,000, Halima Dr 100,000 (2)
4 marks: (d) Femi 900,000 + 66,000 + 60,000 = ₦1,026,000; Gbenga 600,000 + 44,000 + 40,000 = ₦684,000; Halima 700,000 − 100,000 = ₦600,000 (4, deduct 1 per error)
questions.explanation: (a) Revaluation profit = 150,000 − 30,000 − 10,000 = ₦110,000, shared 3:2: Femi ₦66,000 and Gbenga ₦44,000. (b) Femi gets 3/4 x 3/5 = 9/20, Gbenga 3/4 x 2/5 = 6/20 and Halima 1/4 = 5/20, a ratio of 9:6:5. (c) Goodwill of ₦400,000 is credited to the old partners in 3:2 (240,000 and 160,000) and then written off in the new ratio 9:6:5 (180,000, 120,000 and 100,000), a net gain of ₦60,000 to Femi and ₦40,000 to Gbenga paid for by Halima. (d) Closing capitals: Femi ₦1,026,000, Gbenga ₦684,000 and Halima ₦600,000.

questions.stem:
Extracts from the accounts of Sahel Foods Plc for the year are given below.
Revenue ₦8,400,000; cost of sales ₦5,880,000; operating expenses ₦1,260,000
10% debentures ₦2,000,000
Ordinary shares of ₦1 each ₦6,000,000; 8% preference shares ₦1,000,000; retained earnings ₦1,500,000
Current assets ₦2,700,000 (including inventory ₦900,000); current liabilities ₦1,500,000
Assume company income tax at 30% of profit before tax.
Calculate:
(a) gross profit margin [2 marks]
(b) profit before interest and tax, and profit after tax [4 marks]
(c) earnings per ordinary share, in kobo to two decimal places [3 marks]
(d) current ratio and acid test ratio [4 marks]
(e) return on capital employed, taking capital employed as equity plus debentures [2 marks]
questions.explanation: (a) Gross profit is ₦2,520,000, a margin of 30%. (b) PBIT = 2,520,000 − 1,260,000 = ₦1,260,000; less debenture interest ₦200,000 gives PBT ₦1,060,000; tax at 30% is ₦318,000, leaving PAT ₦742,000. (c) Earnings for ordinary shareholders = 742,000 − 80,000 preference dividend = ₦662,000; EPS = 662,000/6,000,000 = 11.03 kobo. (d) Current ratio = 1.8:1; acid test = 1,800,000/1,500,000 = 1.2:1. (e) Capital employed = 6,000,000 + 1,000,000 + 1,500,000 + 2,000,000 = ₦10,500,000; ROCE = 12%.

questions.stem:
Bright Stores has two departments, X and Y. For the year:
Sales: X ₦1,800,000; Y ₦1,200,000
Cost of goods sold: X ₦1,170,000; Y ₦840,000
Expenses: rent ₦360,000; wages ₦400,000; advertising ₦150,000; electricity ₦90,000
Bases of apportionment: rent and electricity by floor area (X 300 m², Y 200 m²); wages by number of staff (X 5, Y 3); advertising by sales.
(a) Apportion the expenses between the departments. [6 marks]
(b) Calculate the net profit or loss of each department. [6 marks]
(c) Should Department Y be closed? Give one reason. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) Rent X 216,000, Y 144,000; wages X 250,000, Y 150,000; advertising X 90,000, Y 60,000; electricity X 54,000, Y 36,000 (deduct 1 per error)
6 marks: (b) X: gross profit 630,000 − expenses 610,000 = net profit ₦20,000 (3); Y: gross profit 360,000 − expenses 390,000 = net loss ₦30,000 (3)
3 marks: (c) Not necessarily (1): Y earns a gross profit of 360,000 that covers part of shared fixed costs such as rent which would remain if Y closed; closing Y could reduce overall profit (2)
questions.explanation: (a) Rent and electricity are shared 3:2 by floor area (rent 216,000 and 144,000; electricity 54,000 and 36,000), wages 5:3 by staff (250,000 and 150,000) and advertising 3:2 by sales (90,000 and 60,000). (b) X earns gross profit of ₦630,000 against expenses of ₦610,000, a net profit of ₦20,000; Y earns ₦360,000 against ₦390,000, a net loss of ₦30,000. (c) Y should not be closed simply because of the loss: much of its apportioned cost, such as rent, would continue, and its gross profit contributes towards those shared costs.

questions.stem:
Head office sends goods to its Jos branch at cost plus 25%, and the branch sells at the invoice price. For the year: goods sent to branch at invoice price ₦1,000,000; branch stock at 1 January (invoice price) ₦150,000; branch stock at 31 December (invoice price) ₦200,000; branch sales (all cash) ₦900,000; branch expenses ₦95,000.
(a) Calculate the loading included in goods sent to the branch. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the closing stock at cost. [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the stock shortage at invoice price and at cost. [4 marks]
(d) Calculate the branch gross profit. [3 marks]
(e) Calculate the branch net profit. [2 marks]
(f) State two reasons for keeping separate branch accounts. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) 1,000,000 x 25/125 = ₦200,000 (2)
2 marks: (b) 200,000 x 100/125 = ₦160,000 (2)
4 marks: (c) 150,000 + 1,000,000 − 900,000 − 200,000 = ₦50,000 at invoice price (2); at cost 50,000 x 100/125 = ₦40,000 (2)
3 marks: (d) Loading on goods sold: 900,000 x 25/125 = ₦180,000 (3)
2 marks: (e) 180,000 − 40,000 − 95,000 = ₦45,000 (2)
2 marks: (f) Any two, 1 mark each: to know the profitability of each branch; to control stock and detect shortages; to assess branch managers; to aid decisions to expand or close branches
questions.explanation: (a) Loading is one-fifth of invoice price: 1,000,000 x 25/125 = ₦200,000. (b) Closing stock at cost = 200,000 x 100/125 = ₦160,000. (c) Expected closing stock at invoice price = 150,000 + 1,000,000 − 900,000 = 250,000, but actual is 200,000, a shortage of ₦50,000 at invoice price or ₦40,000 at cost. (d) Goods sold at cost = 900,000 x 100/125 = 720,000, so gross profit = ₦180,000. (e) Net profit = 180,000 − 40,000 shortage − 95,000 expenses = ₦45,000. (f) Branch accounts show each branch's profitability, control stock and cash, and help assess managers and decide on expansion.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between public sector accounting and private sector accounting. [4 marks]
(b) State four sources of revenue of the Federal Government of Nigeria. [4 marks]
(c) Distinguish between capital expenditure and recurrent expenditure, giving two examples of each. [5 marks]
(d) State the function of the Accountant-General of the Federation. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) Any two, 2 marks each: public sector aims at service and accountability, private sector at profit; public sector funds come from taxes and are controlled by appropriation laws, private from owners and lenders; public sector often uses cash/modified accrual (IPSAS) and fund accounting; no shareholders/dividends in public sector
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: oil and gas revenue (royalties, petroleum profits tax); company income tax; value added tax; customs and excise duties; fees, fines and licences; dividends from government investments; loans and grants
5 marks: (c) Capital expenditure: spending on assets of lasting benefit, e.g. roads, hospitals, schools (2.5); recurrent expenditure: regular running costs, e.g. salaries, overheads, maintenance (2.5)
2 marks: (d) Chief accounting officer of the Federation: manages government accounts and prepares the annual financial statements of the Federation (2)
questions.explanation: (a) Public sector accounting records the receipt and use of public funds under appropriation laws, focusing on accountability and service rather than profit, while private sector accounting measures profit for owners. (b) Federal revenue comes from oil and gas, company income tax, VAT, customs and excise duties, fees, fines and licences, and returns on investments. (c) Capital expenditure creates long-lasting assets such as roads and hospitals; recurrent expenditure covers regular costs such as salaries and maintenance. (d) The Accountant-General manages the Federation's accounts and prepares its financial statements, while the Auditor-General audits them.

questions.stem:
Danladi bought a generator on hire purchase on 1 January Year 1. The cash price was ₦2,400,000. He paid a deposit of ₦600,000 and agreed to pay three annual instalments of ₦750,000 each at the end of every year. Interest is to be allocated using the sum-of-the-years'-digits method. The generator is depreciated at 20% per annum on cash price (straight line).
(a) Calculate the total hire purchase price. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the total interest. [2 marks]
(c) Allocate the interest to Years 1, 2 and 3. [6 marks]
(d) Calculate the depreciation for Year 1 and the net book value at the end of Year 1. [3 marks]
(e) State one difference between hire purchase and credit sale. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) 600,000 + 3 x 750,000 = ₦2,850,000 (2)
2 marks: (b) 2,850,000 − 2,400,000 = ₦450,000 (2)
6 marks: (c) Sum of digits 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 (1.5); Year 1 3/6 x 450,000 = ₦225,000 (1.5); Year 2 2/6 x 450,000 = ₦150,000 (1.5); Year 3 1/6 x 450,000 = ₦75,000 (1.5)
3 marks: (d) Depreciation 20% x 2,400,000 = ₦480,000 (2); NBV = ₦1,920,000 (1)
2 marks: (e) Under hire purchase ownership passes on payment of the last instalment, while under credit sale it passes immediately (2)
questions.explanation: (a) HP price = deposit 600,000 + 3 x 750,000 = ₦2,850,000. (b) Interest = 2,850,000 − 2,400,000 = ₦450,000. (c) With digits summing to 6, Year 1 bears 3/6 (₦225,000), Year 2 2/6 (₦150,000) and Year 3 1/6 (₦75,000), so more interest falls in the early years when more is owed. (d) Depreciation = 20% of ₦2,400,000 = ₦480,000, leaving a book value of ₦1,920,000. (e) Under hire purchase the hirer becomes owner only after the last instalment; under credit sale ownership passes at once.

questions.stem:
Ngozi of Onitsha consigned 500 cartons of detergent, costing ₦4,000 each, to Tobi of Ibadan. Ngozi paid freight and insurance of ₦150,000. Tobi paid carriage to his warehouse of ₦50,000 and selling expenses of ₦30,000. Tobi sold 400 cartons at ₦6,000 each. He is entitled to a commission of 5% on sales plus a del credere commission of 2% on sales.
(a) Calculate Tobi's total commission. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate the value of the unsold stock, including a proportion of expenses incurred before sale. [4 marks]
(c) Calculate the profit on consignment. [6 marks]
(d) What is a del credere commission? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) 7% x 2,400,000 (sales) = ₦168,000 (5% = 120,000; 2% = 48,000) (3)
4 marks: (b) Cost per carton 4,000 + (150,000 + 50,000)/500 = 4,400 (2); 100 x 4,400 = ₦440,000 (2)
6 marks: (c) Sales 2,400,000 + stock 440,000 = 2,840,000 (2); less cost 2,000,000, freight 150,000, carriage 50,000, selling expenses 30,000, commission 168,000 = 2,398,000 (2); profit ₦442,000 (2)
2 marks: (d) Extra commission paid to the consignee for guaranteeing payment by credit customers, so he bears any bad debts (2)
questions.explanation: (a) Commission = 5% + 2% of sales of ₦2,400,000 = ₦168,000. (b) Expenses incurred before sale (freight 150,000 and carriage 50,000) add ₦400 to each carton, so 100 unsold cartons are valued at 100 x ₦4,400 = ₦440,000; selling expenses are excluded. (c) Profit = 2,400,000 + 440,000 − 2,000,000 − 150,000 − 50,000 − 30,000 − 168,000 = ₦442,000. (d) A del credere commission is an extra commission paid to the consignee for bearing the risk of bad debts on credit sales.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a financial system? [3 marks]
(b) Distinguish between the money market and the capital market, giving two instruments traded in each. [6 marks]
(c) Explain three methods by which a company can raise funds from the capital market. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) The network of financial institutions, markets, instruments and regulators through which funds are mobilised from savers and channelled to borrowers (3)
6 marks: (b) Money market deals in short-term funds (up to one year), e.g. treasury bills, commercial papers, certificates of deposit (3); capital market deals in medium- and long-term funds, e.g. shares, bonds, debentures (3)
6 marks: (c) Any three, 2 marks each: offer for subscription (direct to public through prospectus); offer for sale (through an issuing house); rights issue (to existing shareholders in proportion); private placement (to selected investors); bonus issue does not raise cash and is not accepted
questions.explanation: (a) A financial system is the set of institutions (banks, insurance firms, exchanges), markets, instruments and regulators (CBN, SEC, NAICOM) that move funds from savers to users. (b) The money market handles short-term funds through instruments such as treasury bills and commercial papers; the capital market handles long-term funds through shares, bonds and debentures. (c) Companies raise capital by an offer for subscription direct to the public, an offer for sale through an issuing house, a rights issue to existing shareholders, or a private placement with selected investors.

questions.topic: The Accounting Equation and Double Entry Principles
questions.stem:
Uche started business on 1 May with ₦500,000 cash as capital. During May:
1. Bought goods for cash ₦120,000.
2. Bought equipment on credit from Ola Ltd ₦200,000.
3. Sold goods costing ₦80,000 for ₦110,000 cash.
4. Paid Ola Ltd ₦150,000.
5. Withdrew ₦20,000 cash for private use.
(a) State the accounting equation. [2 marks]
(b) Show the effect of each transaction on assets, liabilities and capital. [10 marks]
(c) Calculate total assets, liabilities and capital at 31 May and show that the equation holds. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Assets = Capital + Liabilities (2)
10 marks: (b) 2 marks each: (1) stock +120,000, cash −120,000, no change in totals; (2) assets +200,000, liabilities +200,000; (3) cash +110,000, stock −80,000, capital (profit) +30,000; (4) cash −150,000, liabilities −150,000; (5) cash −20,000, capital −20,000
3 marks: (c) Assets ₦560,000 (1); liabilities ₦50,000 (1); capital ₦510,000; 560,000 = 510,000 + 50,000 (1)
questions.explanation: (a) Assets = Capital + Liabilities. (b) Buying goods for cash swaps one asset for another; buying equipment on credit raises assets and liabilities by ₦200,000; selling goods costing ₦80,000 for ₦110,000 raises assets and capital by the profit of ₦30,000; paying Ola reduces cash and liabilities by ₦150,000; drawings reduce cash and capital by ₦20,000. (c) Assets = 500,000 + 200,000 + 30,000 − 150,000 − 20,000 = ₦560,000; liabilities = ₦50,000; capital = 500,000 + 30,000 − 20,000 = ₦510,000, and 560,000 = 510,000 + 50,000.
